learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparison of numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected 60 percent and locked it in.
observations.exploration: Show winner emails at ten percent spam displayed six spam and nine real, forty percent posterior. End fifty percent spam displayed thirty spam and five real, eighty-six percent. Home restored ten and forty. Toggled all-email view then filtered again, restoring six/nine.
observations.reveal: Corrected to forty percent by six of fifteen, compared sixfold word likelihood with nine-to-one real-mail prevalence, referenced tested fifty-percent case and named naive Bayes use of both prior and evidence.
observations.visual: Actual dark 1257 by 936 screenshots inspected. Hundred-dot grid used filled spam, hollow real and white matching rings, with dimmed nonmatches. Six/nine and thirty/five counts matched visible highlighted groups; compact reveal text legible.
observations.previewIsolation: Preview banner said history and analytics are not saved.
observations.blinding: No source, builder notes or other reviews inspected.

prediction.reason: Concrete conditional-probability question targets reversing likelihood and posterior.
prediction.evidence: Sixty percent word frequency versus forty percent posterior.

interaction.reason: Filtering and reversible base-rate endpoints show denominator changes.
interaction.evidence: Same word rates yield forty versus eighty-six percent.

payoff.reason: Reveal grounds calculation in natural frequencies and explains prevalence.
payoff.evidence: Six of fifteen matching messages are spam.

clarity.reason: Shape and ring encodings plus explicit invented rates support interpretation.
clarity.evidence: Filled, hollow and ring legend; hundred-email grid.

transfer.reason: Spam-filter usefulness named, but no new application beyond same email case.
transfer.evidence: Naive Bayes mention alone does not test transfer.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard prevalence endpoints and text counts observed; screen reader, contrast and reduced motion unaudited.

surprise.reason: A strongly spam-associated word can still match more real messages.
surprise.evidence: Nine real matches versus six spam at low base rate.

visualExplanation.reason: Natural-frequency grid exposes the competing sources of word matches.
visualExplanation.evidence: Ring subset across filled and hollow dots.

playfulness.reason: Filtering and prevalence slider support direct comparison.

practicalValue.evidence: Prior prevalence matters despite predictive word.

depth.reason: Likelihood ratio, prior odds and posterior are connected without formula overload.
depth.evidence: Sixfold evidence versus nine-to-one starting odds.

complexity.reason: Countable grid supports unfamiliar conditional-probability reasoning.
complexity.conceptualDemand: Distinguish word given spam from spam given word and account for base rate.
complexity.interfaceBurden: One filter toggle and one prevalence slider.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Prior prevalence and likelihood versus posterior.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: Percentages, six-of-fifteen ratio and odds language.

whyCool: A predictive word can still occur in more real mail when real mail is common.
caveat: Rates are invented and one word is isolated; no actual classifier or fresh application was tested.
effort: Approximately 3 minutes of actual browser review.
